title: Before Growth: Find a product users love before chasing growth targets
summary: Altman argues that Silicon Valley startups set weekly growth goals before knowing what they're building. Founders should first figure out what they're doing, build something some users love enough to spontaneously recommend, and only then focus on growth above all else.

principles.text: Sequence matters: figure out what you're doing, build a product some users love, then focus on growth above all else.
principles.quote: In the first few weeks of a startup’s life, the founders really need to figure out what they’re doing and why. Then they need to build a product some users really love. Only after that they should focus on growth above all else.

principles.text: Premature growth targets produce a nebulous product, masked by growth hacking until retention numbers expose it.
principles.quote: A startup that prematurely targets a growth goal often ends up making a nebulous product that some users sort of like and papering over this with ‘growth hacking’.

principles.text: The right initial metric: do any users love it so much they spontaneously tell others to use it?
principles.quote: I think the right initial metric is “do any users love our product so much they spontaneously tell other people to use it?” Until that’s a “yes”, founders are generally better off focusing on this instead of a growth target.

principles.text: No amount of growth hacking can turn a product nobody loves into a great company.
principles.quote: if you don’t figure it out, no amount of growth hacking will make you into a great company.

principles.text: Great companies usually pass the 'users love it' binary test before turning all their energy to growth.
principles.quote: The very best technology companies sometimes take awhile to figure out exactly what they’re doing, but when they do, they usually pass that binary test before turning all their energy to growth.

principles.text: Startups without a loved product rarely develop the sense of mission the best companies have.
principles.quote: startups that don’t first figure out a product some users love also seem to rarely develop the sense of mission that the best companies have.
